description: We are an interdisciplinary team of university students united by one conviction: the science that protects an astronaut millions of miles from home is the same science that can transform health for millions of people here on Earth.
summary: HeMoSo is a health monitoring software for astronauts on long missions. A crew member records twelve indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, core temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood, a 90-second reaction check adapted from NASA’s PVT-B, appetite, fluid intake and body mass), symptoms and pain, and the app compares each reading with that person’s own usual range and with published clinical limits. It returns one of four states in plain words, names who should act (the crew, the crew medical officer on board, or the flight surgeon on the ground), and shows the next step. Possible conditions appear as an evidence score with the signals behind it, never as a percentage and never as a certainty. Every threshold carries its source or is marked as an assumption, on screen. It uses synthetic data, works when the link to Earth is down, and does not replace the medical team.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

A crew member signs in, records what they measured (twelve indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, core temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood, a 90-second reaction check, appetite, fluid intake and body mass), ticks any symptoms, and marks pain or an injury on a 3D body. The app compares each reading with that person’s own usual range and with published clinical limits, and returns one of four states in plain words: no data yet, in your usual range, outside your usual range, or needs review. For each state it names who acts (the crew, the crew medical officer on board, or the flight surgeon on the ground) and shows the next step. Possible conditions appear as an evidence score from 0 to 1 with the signals behind it and the source of each limit, never as a percentage and never as a certainty; a red-flag symptom shows “Call your CMO now” before any score. The history of every indicator is shown as a trend.

HOW IT WORKS

The rules live in plain files a biologist can edit without touching code: the indicator list, the attention limits, the possible conditions with the signals and symptoms they rest on, the symptom list, and one page of text per indicator. A content check validates all of them before every merge. Three rules decide the state. First, a limit with a published source is checked before anything else and needs no history: a core temperature of 39.5 °C is a review on the first day, and a value exactly on a limit counts (“140/90 or higher”). Second, a limit we could not source is marked “Assumption” on screen and never raises an alarm on its own. Third, the person’s own range compares each reading with their last 14 mission days, one value per day, using the median and a robust spread, so one busy day cannot hide a quiet week. Evidence for a condition is a weighted mean of the signals present, plus the symptoms reported, capped so it can never look certain. The API and the app compute the same rules and are tested against the same shared test cases.

BUILT FOR A REAL MISSION

Each indicator names the instrument that measures it on board today, for example the i-STAT blood analyser, the SLAMMD body mass device, CSA’s Bio-Monitor and the ISS Reaction Self Test; our 90-second reaction check is adapted from NASA’s 3-minute PVT-B and says so. The app uses the crew’s own terms (Flight Day, GMT, post-sleep), keeps every reading on the device when the link to Earth is down and sends it when it returns, and follows the real chain of care: crew, crew medical officer, flight surgeon. It never diagnoses and never replaces the medical team.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

On a long mission the flight surgeon is minutes or hours away. HeMoSo turns a measurement into a next step at the moment it matters, in the crew member’s own language, and tells them who to notify. Every number is traceable to a NASA, CSA, WHO, NIH, AHA or ADA document, or marked as an assumption, which is what makes the output usable by a non-specialist. The same daily check works wherever the doctor is far away: Antarctic stations, offshore rigs, rural clinics.

TOOLS AND STACK

React 19, TypeScript and Vite for the interface, three.js for the 3D body, FastAPI and Python for the API on Railway, PostgreSQL on Supabase with row-level security for storage, and Vercel for the frontend. Accounts use a PIN stored only as a salted scrypt hash; optional face sign-in runs on the device and the face never leaves it. Tests: Vitest, Playwright with axe accessibility checks, pytest and ruff. All data in the app and the deployments is synthetic.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

The comparison is with the person, not with a population, because the same value can be normal for one crew member and not for another, and microgravity changes the baseline. The clinical limits still apply on day one, before any history exists. The “how you are today” state combines reaction, mood and sleep without ever labelling the person. We chose a measured test (the reaction check) over guessing mood from a face. The interface never relies on colour alone, works with the keyboard and a screen reader, and respects reduced motion.
